paragraphs: This is the natural and unavoidable tendency of even the best constituted governments. If Sparta and Rome perished, what State can hope to last forever? If we want to build a form of government that lasts a long time, let us not even dream of making it eternal. To succeed, we must not attempt the impossible, or flatter ourselves that we can give a human creation a stability that the human condition does not allow.

The body politic, like the human body, begins to die from the moment it is born, and carries within itself the causes of its own destruction. But either may have a constitution that is more or less robust and fitted to keep it alive for a longer or shorter time. The constitution of a man is the work of nature; that of the State is the work of art. Men cannot lengthen their own lives; but it is up to them to lengthen the life of the State as far as possible, by giving it the best possible constitution. The best constituted State will come to an end; but it will end later than any other, unless some unforeseen accident destroys it before its time.

The principle of life in the body politic lies in the sovereign authority. The legislative power is the heart of the State; the executive power is its brain, which sets all the parts in motion. The brain may be paralyzed and the individual still live. A man may remain feeble-minded and live; but as soon as the heart stops doing its work, the animal is dead.

The State does not survive by means of the laws, but by means of the legislative power. Yesterday’s law is not binding today; but silence is taken for tacit consent, and the Sovereign is held to be confirming, at every moment, the laws it does not repeal when it could. Whatever it has once declared that it wills, it wills always, unless it revokes the declaration.

Why, then, is so much respect paid to old laws? For this very reason. We must believe that only the excellence of the old acts of will can have preserved them so long: if the Sovereign had not recognized them as wholly beneficial, it would have revoked them a thousand times. This is why, far from growing weak, the laws continually gain new strength in any well constituted State; the precedent of antiquity makes them more venerable every day. Wherever the laws grow weak as they grow old, this proves that there is no longer a legislative power, and that the State is dead.
